claims.text: Conventional HIP treatment of Ta20Nb20Hf20Zr20Ti20 typically produces a continuous B2 matrix.
A continuous B2 matrix causes suboptimal high-temperature ductility.
HIP at approximately 1150 °C followed by rapid, precisely controlled cooling can invert the microstructure from a continuous B2 matrix to a continuous BCC matrix containing discrete B2 precipitates.
The targeted continuous BCC phase is ductile.
The controlled-cooling treatment will produce finely dispersed, discrete B2 precipitates within the continuous BCC matrix.
A continuous BCC matrix will maintain alloy ductility.
Discrete B2 precipitates will act as barriers to dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion will reduce plastic deformation and creep.
The combination of a continuous BCC matrix and discrete B2 precipitates will improve elevated-temperature strength and ductility.
At 1023 K, the optimized alloy will have higher yield strength than a conventionally HIP-treated control with a continuous B2 matrix.
At 1023 K, the optimized alloy will have greater ductility than a conventionally HIP-treated control with a continuous B2 matrix.
The treatment is also expected to improve creep resistance at approximately 1023 K.
The claimed mechanical benefits are bounded to HIP near 1150 °C, optimized controlled cooling, and testing near 750 °C under extreme loading conditions.
The magnitude of improvement is sensitive to cooling control and variability in microstructural evolution.
Reliable formation of the inverted microstructure is necessary for the predicted mechanical improvement.
